BALCONY AND EXTERIOR ELEVATED ELEMENT INSPECTIONS (HEALTH & SAF. CODE § 17973; CIV. CODE § 5551) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for 456 Elm St., Berkeley, CA 94704 · Elm Street Apartments LLC / Elm Street Condominium Owners Association

PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes California's two statutory inspection programs for wood-framed balconies, decks, stairways, walkways, and similar "exterior elevated elements" on multifamily buildings, as they may apply to the building at 456 Elm St., Berkeley, CA 94704, for which Elm Street Apartments LLC / Elm Street Condominium Owners Association is identified as the building owner or the association responsible for maintenance, and as provided to Jordan Lee. It states what Health and Safety Code § 17973 (added by SB 721 in 2018) provides for apartment and other non-condominium buildings with three or more multifamily dwelling units, what Civil Code § 5551 (added by SB 326 in 2019) provides for condominium projects governed by the Davis-Stirling Common Interest Development Act, what each statute says about who performs the inspection, what the inspection and the written report must contain, the deadlines, the handling of an element found to pose an immediate threat to occupant safety, the repair, penalty, and lien provisions, and the related record-retention and transfer-disclosure rules. It does not determine whether 456 Elm St., Berkeley, CA 94704 is subject to either statute, whether any inspection of that building has been performed or was adequate, or what any person should do about a particular balcony, deck, or report.

APARTMENT BUILDINGS: WHICH BUILDINGS MUST BE INSPECTED AND WHO MAY PERFORM THE INSPECTION (HEALTH & SAF. CODE § 17973(A), (N))
Health and Safety Code § 17973, added in 2018 by SB 721 (Stats. 2018, Ch. 445), requires that exterior elevated elements that include load-bearing components be inspected in all buildings containing three or more multifamily dwelling units. The inspection may be performed only by one of the professionals the statute lists: a licensed architect; a licensed civil or structural engineer; a building contractor holding an "A," "B," or "C-5" license classification from the Contractors State License Board with at least five years' experience, as a holder of those classifications, constructing multistory wood-frame buildings; or an individual certified as a building inspector or building official by a recognized state, national, or international association, as determined by the local jurisdiction. The inspector may not be employed by the local jurisdiction while performing the inspection, and must be hired by the building owner. The statute describes the purpose of the inspection as determining that the elements and their associated waterproofing are in a generally safe condition, in adequate working order, and free from any hazardous condition caused by fungus, deterioration, decay, or improper alteration to the extent that life, limb, health, property, safety, or welfare of the public or the occupants is not endangered. Subdivision (n) provides that the section does not apply to a common interest development as defined in Civil Code § 4100; condominium projects are instead addressed by Civil Code § 5551, described later in this sheet.

APARTMENT BUILDINGS: WHAT COUNTS AS AN "EXTERIOR ELEVATED ELEMENT" (HEALTH & SAF. CODE § 17973(B))
Section 17973(b) defines the three terms that fix the statute's reach. An "exterior elevated element" is any of the listed structure types -- balconies, decks, porches, stairways, walkways, and entry structures, including their supports and railings -- that extends beyond the building's exterior walls, has a walking surface elevated more than six feet above ground level, is designed for human occupancy or use, and relies in whole or in substantial part on wood or wood-based products for its structural support or stability. "Load-bearing components" are the components that extend beyond the exterior walls to deliver structural loads from the element to the building. "Associated waterproofing elements" include the flashings, membranes, coatings, and sealants that protect those load-bearing components from exposure to water and the elements. Read together with subdivision (a), the inspection duty attaches to elements that include load-bearing components; an elevated element that is not wood-based, or whose walking surface is six feet or less above ground level, falls outside the definition.

APARTMENT BUILDINGS: MINIMUM CONTENTS OF THE INSPECTION AND THE WRITTEN REPORT (HEALTH & SAF. CODE § 17973(C))
Section 17973(c) sets the minimum content of the inspection. The inspector must identify each type of exterior elevated element that, if defective, decayed, or deteriorated to the point of not meeting its load requirements, would in the inspector's opinion threaten the occupants' health or safety, and must assess the load-bearing components and associated waterproofing of those elements by direct visual examination or comparable means. The statute fixes a minimum sample: at least 15 percent of each type of exterior elevated element must be inspected. The evaluation must address, as of its date, the elements' current condition, expectations of future performance and projected service life, and recommendations for any further inspection. The inspector must then present a written report, stamped or signed, to the owner or the owner's designated agent within 45 days after completing the inspection. The report must include photographs, any test results, and narrative sufficient to establish a baseline that later inspections can be compared against, and must state which, if any, element poses an immediate threat to occupant safety and whether preventing occupant access or emergency repairs, including shoring, are necessary.

APARTMENT BUILDINGS: INSPECTION DEADLINES, THE SIX-YEAR CYCLE, NEWER BUILDINGS, ASBESTOS, AND RECORD RETENTION (HEALTH & SAF. CODE § 17973(D)-(F))
Under § 17973(d)(1), the inspection must be completed by January 1, 2026, and by January 1 every six years thereafter. As enacted in 2018 the initial deadline was January 1, 2025; AB 2579 (2024) extended it to January 1, 2026, and the Legislative Counsel's Digest for that bill describes the extension. The same paragraph requires the inspector to produce an initial report and, at the owner's request, a final report indicating that required repairs were completed; requires later reports to incorporate copies of prior reports with the locations of the elements inspected; allows local enforcement agencies to require additional report content and submission of the initial or final reports; and requires the owner to keep copies of all inspection reports in the building's permanent records for at least two inspection cycles and to disclose and deliver them to the buyer at any later sale of the building. Paragraph (d)(2), added in 2025, addresses asbestos: if the owner confirms the presence of asbestos-containing material during the inspection and cannot complete the inspection as a result, the owner has up to nine months to complete abatement under applicable law and then no more than three months to complete the inspection, and must keep records of the asbestos and its abatement for three years after the inspection. For a building whose building-permit application was submitted on or after January 1, 2019, subdivision (e) requires the inspection no later than six years after the local jurisdiction issues a certificate of occupancy. Subdivision (f) provides that a building inspected within three years before January 1, 2019 by a qualified inspector, with a report stating the elements were in proper working condition and posed no threat to public health and safety, needed no new inspection until January 1, 2026.

APARTMENT BUILDINGS: ELEMENTS POSING AN IMMEDIATE THREAT, EMERGENCY MEASURES, AND REPAIR TIMELINES (HEALTH & SAF. CODE § 17973(D)(1), (G), (H))
Section 17973 treats an element the inspector identifies as an immediate threat differently from one needing ordinary corrective work. Under subdivision (d)(1), a copy of any report that recommends immediate repairs, advises that a building assembly poses an immediate threat to occupant safety, or states that preventing occupant access or emergency repairs (including shoring) are necessary must be provided by the inspector to both the owner and the local enforcement agency within 15 days after the report is completed. Under subdivision (h)(1), such an element is an "emergency condition," and the owner must perform the required preventive measures immediately; the statute states that immediately preventing occupant access to the element until emergency repairs can be completed constitutes compliance with that paragraph. Emergency repairs must comply with subdivision (g), be inspected by the inspector, and be reported to the local enforcement agency. For corrective work the inspector says does not pose an immediate threat, subdivision (h)(2) requires the owner to apply for a permit within 120 days after receiving the report and, once the permit is approved, to make the repairs within 120 days unless the local enforcement agency grants an extension. Subdivision (g) requires every element found to need repair or replacement to be corrected by the owner, with all necessary permits obtained from the local jurisdiction, and all work performed by a qualified and licensed contractor in compliance with the inspector's recommendations, any applicable manufacturer's specifications, the California Building Standards Code (consistent with Health and Safety Code § 17922(d)), and all local requirements.

APARTMENT BUILDINGS: OWNER RESPONSIBILITY, CIVIL PENALTIES, BUILDING SAFETY LIENS, AND ENFORCEMENT COSTS (HEALTH & SAF. CODE § 17973(I)-(L))
Section 17973(i)(1) places responsibility for compliance on the building owner, and subdivision (k) makes the continued and ongoing maintenance of exterior elevated elements in a safe and functional condition the owner's responsibility. If the owner does not comply with the repair requirements within 180 days, subdivision (i)(2) requires the inspector to notify the local enforcement agency and the owner; if the repairs are not completed within 30 days after that notice, the owner is to be assessed a civil penalty, under a fee schedule set by the local authority, of not less than $100 nor more than $500 per day until the repairs are completed, unless the local enforcement agency grants an extension. When a civil penalty is assessed, subdivision (i)(3) permits the local jurisdiction to record a "building safety lien" in the county recorder's office, which from the date of recording has the force, effect, and priority of a judgment lien. Subdivision (j) prescribes the lien's contents (amount, agency, street address, legal description and assessor's parcel number, and the recorded owner's name and address), requires a recorded notice of discharge when the lien is satisfied, provides that the lien may be foreclosed by an action for a money judgment brought by the local jurisdiction, and allows recording-cost recovery. Subdivision (l) states that local enforcement agencies may recover enforcement costs associated with the section's requirements.

APARTMENT BUILDINGS: CONDOMINIUM CONVERSIONS, STRICTER LOCAL ORDINANCES, AND LANDLORD ENTRY TO COMPLY (HEALTH & SAF. CODE § 17973(M), (O); CIV. CODE § 1954(A)(6))
Three further provisions round out the apartment-building program. First, under § 17973(m), a covered building proposed for conversion to condominiums to be sold to the public after January 1, 2019 must be inspected before the first close of escrow of a separate interest in the project; the report must include the inspector's recommendations for repair or replacement of any element found defective, decayed, or deteriorated to the point of not meeting its load requirements, and the report together with the inspector's written confirmation that recommended repairs were completed must be submitted to the Department of Real Estate as a condition of the final public report, included with the written statement of defects required by Civil Code § 1134, provided to the local jurisdiction, and made a condition of the local jurisdiction's final inspection or certificate of occupancy. Second, subdivision (o) allows the governing body of any city, county, or city and county to enact ordinances imposing requirements greater than the statute's. Health and Safety Code § 17973, added in 2018 by SB 721 (Stats. 2018, Ch. 445), requires that exterior elevated elements that include load-bearing components be inspected in all buildings containing three or more multifamily dwelling units. The inspection may be performed only by one of the professionals the statute lists: a licensed architect; a licensed civil or structural engineer; a building contractor holding an "A," "B," or "C-5" license classification from the Contractors State License Board with at least five years' experience, as a holder of those classifications, constructing multistory wood-frame buildings; or an individual certified as a building inspector or building official by a recognized state, national, or international association, as determined by the local jurisdiction. The inspector may not be employed by the local jurisdiction while performing the inspection, and must be hired by the building owner. The statute describes the purpose of the inspection as determining that the elements and their associated waterproofing are in a generally safe condition, in adequate working order, and free from any hazardous condition caused by fungus, deterioration, decay, or improper alteration to the extent that life, limb, health, property, safety, or welfare of the public or the occupants is not endangered. Subdivision (n) provides that the section does not apply to a common interest development as defined in Civil Code § 4100; condominium projects are instead addressed by Civil Code § 5551, described later in this sheet.

expectedJSON.body: Section 17973(b) defines the three terms that fix the statute's reach. An "exterior elevated element" is any of the listed structure types -- balconies, decks, porches, stairways, walkways, and entry structures, including their supports and railings -- that extends beyond the building's exterior walls, has a walking surface elevated more than six feet above ground level, is designed for human occupancy or use, and relies in whole or in substantial part on wood or wood-based products for its structural support or stability. "Load-bearing components" are the components that extend beyond the exterior walls to deliver structural loads from the element to the building. "Associated waterproofing elements" include the flashings, membranes, coatings, and sealants that protect those load-bearing components from exposure to water and the elements. Read together with subdivision (a), the inspection duty attaches to elements that include load-bearing components; an elevated element that is not wood-based, or whose walking surface is six feet or less above ground level, falls outside the definition.

expectedJSON.body: Section 17973(c) sets the minimum content of the inspection. The inspector must identify each type of exterior elevated element that, if defective, decayed, or deteriorated to the point of not meeting its load requirements, would in the inspector's opinion threaten the occupants' health or safety, and must assess the load-bearing components and associated waterproofing of those elements by direct visual examination or comparable means. The statute fixes a minimum sample: at least 15 percent of each type of exterior elevated element must be inspected. The evaluation must address, as of its date, the elements' current condition, expectations of future performance and projected service life, and recommendations for any further inspection. The inspector must then present a written report, stamped or signed, to the owner or the owner's designated agent within 45 days after completing the inspection. The report must include photographs, any test results, and narrative sufficient to establish a baseline that later inspections can be compared against, and must state which, if any, element poses an immediate threat to occupant safety and whether preventing occupant access or emergency repairs, including shoring, are necessary.

expectedJSON.body: For condominium projects, the parallel requirement is Civil Code § 5551, part of the Davis-Stirling Common Interest Development Act, added by SB 326 (Stats. 2019, Ch. 207). At least once every nine years, the board of an association of a condominium project must cause a reasonably competent and diligent visual inspection, by a licensed structural or civil engineer or architect, of a random and statistically significant sample of the exterior elevated elements for which the association has maintenance or repair responsibility. The section applies only to buildings containing three or more attached multifamily dwelling units. Its definitions differ in structure from the Health and Safety Code's: "load-bearing components" are the components extending beyond the exterior walls that deliver structural loads to the building from decks, balconies, stairways, walkways, and their railings, with a walking surface more than six feet above ground level, designed for human occupancy or use, and supported in whole or in substantial part by wood or wood-based products; "exterior elevated elements" means those load-bearing components together with their associated waterproofing system; a "statistically significant sample" is enough units to give 95 percent confidence that the sample reflects the whole, with a margin of error no greater than plus or minus 5 percent; and "visual inspection" means the least intrusive method necessary, including visual observation alone or combined with tools such as moisture meters, borescopes, or infrared technology.

expectedJSON.body: Section 5551 prescribes how the sample is chosen and carried forward. Before the first visual inspection, the inspector must generate a random list of the locations of each type of exterior elevated element, covering every element for which the association has maintenance or repair responsibility, and provide that list to the association for future use. The inspector performs the visual inspections in the order of that list, and each later inspection under the section begins with the next element on the list and proceeds in order. The inspection must determine whether the elements are in a generally safe condition and performing in accordance with applicable standards. If during the visual inspection the inspector observes building conditions indicating that unintended water or water vapor has passed into the associated waterproofing system, creating the potential for damage to the load-bearing components, the inspector may conduct a further inspection, exercising best professional judgment about its necessity, scope, and breadth.

Subdivision (i) required the first inspection to be completed by January 1, 2025, with inspections every nine years thereafter in coordination with the reserve study inspection under § 5550, and requires all written reports to be kept for two inspection cycles as association records. For a building whose building-permit application was submitted on or after January 1, 2020, the inspection must occur no later than six years after the certificate of occupancy is issued. Subdivision (j) places responsibility for compliance on the association and makes the continued maintenance and repair of the load-bearing components and waterproofing systems in a safe, functional, and sanitary condition the association's responsibility as required by its governing documents. The board may adopt rules or bylaws, and a local government or enforcement agency may adopt an ordinance or rule, imposing requirements greater than the statute's.

expectedJSON.body: The same bill that enacted the condominium inspection requirement, SB 326, also added Civil Code § 5986, which addresses an association's ability to pursue construction claims -- including claims about balconies and other exterior elements -- against the developer. Subject to compliance with § 6150 (which requires the board to give members written notice of a meeting to discuss problems that may lead to a civil action at least 30 days before filing, or within 30 days after filing if the association reasonably believes the statute of limitations will otherwise expire), and notwithstanding any contrary provision in the governing documents, the board has authority to commence and pursue a claim, civil action, arbitration, prelitigation process under § 6000 or the Right to Repair Act (Civil Code § 895 et seq.), or other legal proceeding against a declarant, developer, or builder; where the board includes members appointed by or affiliated with the developer, that decision is vested solely in the non-affiliated members. Subdivision (b) declares that governing documents may not impose preconditions or limitations on that authority, and that any such limitation -- including a membership-vote prerequisite or a developer veto -- is unenforceable, null, and void. Subdivision (c) preserves limitations adopted solely by the non-declarant-affiliated members in accordance with the amendment requirements of the governing documents, and subdivision (d) applies the section to governing documents whenever recorded and retroactively to pending claims not already resolved by settlement, final arbitration, or final judgment. Subdivision (e) states that the section does not extend any statute of limitations or repose.
